A novel approach is used to model the interaction between gas and dust, allowing us to simulate the behavior of dust particles in a gravitational environment. By analyzing the evolution of low-metallicity molecular clouds, we identify a previously overlooked phase in the star formation process, characterized by the formation of small dust particles due to supernovae explosions. This phase is shown to significantly impact the development of the star formation process, with the accumulation of dust particles eventually leading to the creation of larger dust grains, albeit at a slower rate than observed in higher-metallicity environments. The time it takes for dust grains to reach a size of 0.1 micrometers by mass is found to be 3-5 million years in the simulated low-metallicity molecular clouds, with this value decreasing to 1-2 million years in clouds with double the metal content. Detecting three-dimensional objects at a distance is a significant obstacle in the 3D detection field, where existing evaluation metrics and evaluation tools fail to accurately reflect the practical applications of this technology.  Far3Det: Towards Distant 3D Detection is a new benchmark designed to address this issue by introducing a new evaluation protocol that mimics real-world scenarios, along with a Far3Det dataset based on the KITTI dataset, which serves as a foundation for advancing 3D detection beyond current range limitations.  A pre-trained PointRCNN model, adapted to the Far3Det dataset, serves as the initial entry for this challenge, and the competition invites participants to submit their own distance-aware 3D detection algorithms for evaluation against this benchmark.  A distinct feature of the Far3Det dataset is the distinct classification of detected objects into near and distant categories, based on their Euclidean distances to the sensor, which poses a significant challenge for participating algorithms in achieving a balance between precision and recall in their predictions.  The evaluation of submitted entries will be based on the average precision of distant detection, along with other performance metrics, which will be calculated across multiple scenes in the dataset.  The Far3Det competition aims to tackle the longstanding challenge of distant 3D detection in the field and to explore novel solutions to this problem.  Due to the restricted size of the dataset, the competition will employ a closed-door participation approach, where participation is limited to a select group of top-performing teams in the KITTI 3D detection competition, which serves as a prerequisite for consideration.  The introduction of the Far3Det dataset and its associated protocol is anticipated to drive advancements in 3D detection beyond current range limitations, which is a critical capability for the development of safe and reliable autonomous vehicles.  The Far3Det competition will provide a platform for researchers to explore novel solutions to the distant 3D detection problem, which is a critical problem in the field.  The code, model, and dataset of the Far3Det competition are available at https://github.com/leiming1994/Far3Det.  The evaluation board of the competition is open to receive new entries until May 31, 2023, and the final results will be published at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2023. Chemical reactions in complex organic molecules are influenced by their electronic structure. To understand reaction dynamics, it's essential to have a well-trained machine learning model that can accurately represent the ground state of the molecule, even with high energy levels. By utilizing quantum simulated properties of the molecule's electronic structure, we can train a learning algorithm to create a classical model that effectively captures the ground state behavior across isoelectronic molecules sharing similar geometry. Our study demonstrates the potential of combining quantum simulation and machine learning to efficiently explore reaction pathways in molecules. In neurosurgery, haptic-enabled patient-specific models are utilized for precise brain tissue registration. This process involves mapping a precise anatomical volume onto the patient's brain surface for better surgical navigation. However, adapting these models for non-linear alignments proves challenging due to the high dimensionality of the data. We have developed a novel surface-to-volume alignment technique that leverages a biomechanical model informed by clinical data to accommodate non-linear transformations. This approach facilitates the discovery of a flexible surface that matches a given volumetric data set, with the constraint that the surface remains intact. By formulating this problem as an optimal transport challenge and solving it using a linearized version, our algorithm successfully handles complex alignments. Our method surpasses the limitations of previous surface-to-volume alignment techniques that solely employ linear least squares methods, and our results demonstrate its effectiveness in processing large-scale medical datasets. Our algorithm also exhibits efficiency, with the ability to process over 3 million triangles in under an hour on a standard computer. This implies that it can accurately determine non-linear alignments in reasonable time, even for large-scale medical datasets. Our method holds significant potential for enhancing brain registration algorithms. Our project's code is publicly available for use and review at https://github.com/amirarad/3DRegistration. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. However, estimating scene flow is challenging due to the complex nature of real-world scenarios and the presence of ambiguous density in areas where objects meet. Traditional approaches typically leverage metric learning to pretrain their models on datasets with annotated data, relying on neighboring points to constrain estimates and reducing the difficulty of the estimation problem. In contrast, our proposed method trains a model in an adversarial manner to directly estimate scene flow from image data, thus eliminating the need for intermediate two-dimensional processing steps. By utilizing a flow-based metric that is learned simultaneously, our model produces scene flow estimates that are both spatially coherent and accurate. In experiments, our results demonstrate improved estimator robustness and the benefits of a self-guided estimation process, with our method achieving superior performance on certain datasets and challenging benchmark scenes. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/kuangdada/Advsmlsf. Furthermore, our model was found to be particularly effective for estimating motion in areas with turbulent fluid dynamics and complex deformations. In particular, our method outperformed prior approaches on the NTU-RGB-D Flow dataset and in scenarios mimicking rainy and foggy conditions, while also exhibiting a reasonable compromise between computational burden and achieved accuracy. In addition, our method shows that spatial coherence can be achieved without relying on neighboring points through the use of a learned metric. The model's ability to estimate motion in challenging situations is demonstrated through the inclusion of additional demonstration videos in the supplementary material. By comparing the thermodynamic properties of spin-aligned strange quark matter with those of spin-unaligned strange quark matter, we determined the critical density at which deconfinement occurs and found the stability of spin-aligned strange quark matter to be more robust. Furthermore, we derived the equation governing spin-aligned strange quark stars and found their mass spectrum to exhibit an increase with magnetic field strength, temperature, and quark chemical potential, while temperature and quark chemical potential cause the star's radius to expand. At zero temperature and magnetic field, our findings align with existing literature. We validated the model by analyzing the static and vector meson mass spectrum and observed the emergence of meson mass values consistent with experimental data in the absence of a magnetic field. Additionally, we analyzed the general properties of spin-aligned strange quark stars and found them to resemble their antiparticle counterparts. Our calculations indicate that stars exhibiting spin-aligned properties may exhibit unique features, such as crust layers composed of superconducting and superfluid phases, and that magnetic field effects on the star's density distribution may vary based on the density of the quark matter. We validated our model against observational data from compact stars with low magnetic fields and found the results to be consistent with the model's parameters. To model defected graphene, we utilize the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger ladder model, modified to accommodate both lattice defects and dopant impurities. By integrating the model with a thermal bath represented by phonons, we incorporate temperature effects and investigate the magnetic shielding both theoretically and through a numerical approach. Our findings show that temperature significantly impacts the shielding phenomenon, potentially altering it from a positive to a negative response in the presence of heat. This phenomenon is especially evident in the case of dopant impurities. Furthermore, we observe that the heat capacity of the system is closely correlated with the shielding in the high-temperature range. However, the influence of temperature on the shielding near the Fermi level varies greatly depending on the type of defect. While a positive shielding effect is a hallmark of the Fermi level in the case of lattice defects, it is not necessarily the case for defects that break orbital symmetry. The distinct behavior of shielding near the Fermi level in different defects implies that the electronic structure of the material must be considered in the assessment of suitable substitutional impurities. The proposed model can also be applied to investigate the shielding in other systems with electronic structure similar to that of graphene. The method employs the finite-temperature Gutzwiller approach and can be numerically simulated using a thermodynamic cycle Monte Carlo method. The results obtained from this method are verified by comparison with experimental data on the heat capacity of doped graphene samples. A potential solution to this issue may lie in the use of a novel type of activation function called the Modulated Recurrent Activation (MRA) unit, which is based on the principle of repeated application of a transformation over time. The initial condition is learned through a process of backwards iteration that begins from the output layer and moves backwards to the input layer, with each layer's parameters serving as a form of data that informs the next layer's behavior. As a result, the MRA unit is able to generate latent features that not only capture the universal structures present in the data but also the unique local structures present in each individual dataset. To overcome this limitation, robots must be able to efficiently learn from multiple instructors, even if those instructors provide guidance that may be incorrect or inconsistent. In this paper, we introduce a groundbreaking concept - the idea that humans naturally understand the target task in a categorical manner, which we refer to as a "family of solutions." We argue that by recognizing this underlying structure, we can develop a robust learning algorithm capable of interpreting and incorporating both accurate and inaccurate guidance in a nuanced way. This algorithm utilizes a novel hybrid loss function that simultaneously leverages both human input and its corresponding corrective feedback in a flexible manner. As a result, our method can effectively learn from human guidance, even when that guidance is flawed, and enables our robots to generalize their learning across a variety of scenarios. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a series of challenging grasping tasks, showcasing that a single model can accurately learn to perform a variety of different tasks by combining feedback from multiple instructors. Furthermore, our method anticipates that human instructors will provide both high-quality and low-quality guidance, which we refer to as the "strong form" and the "weak form" of our algorithm respectively. Under the "weak form," our algorithm can learn to perform a task even when the human instructor provides no corrective feedback on incorrect actions, a scenario that we test through a series of searching tasks. In addition to presenting our method, we also introduce a new evaluation metric called the "human-robot Loops," which measures the number of human-robot interactions required to reach a certain level of task performance. By comparing the decay of Al$^{3+}$ ion spins with and without NV center protons, we gather substantial evidence for the impact of inter-orbital coupling on the Al$^{3+}$ ion's behavior. Furthermore, we illustrate that this interaction may be utilized to devise novel methods for detecting the presence of protons in diamond, potentially including chemical structure analysis through dynamic nuclear polarization. Additionally, our findings facilitate the development of more precise experiments aimed at studying the Al$^{3+}$ ion's physics.

In the context of urban transportation, the interaction between individuals within confined public transportation settings has the potential to significantly impact the spread of illness across an urban area. Considering the long duration of bus trips and the confined spaces on board, the transmission dynamics in this environment may diverge from those observed in other gathering places. We investigate the spread of a contagious illness among urban bus passengers using a range of modeling approaches, including a well-mixed model that assumes an equilibrium between people entering and leaving the bus. Our analysis shows that the spread of illness is highly dependent on the number of individuals transferring between buses, with the likelihood of a major outbreak being lower on short buses with frequent departures. Furthermore, we find that the spread of illness is more effectively mitigated by reducing the number of people transferring between buses than by increasing the distance between urban bus stops. The results of our study have implications for the development of strategies to manage the transmission of infectious diseases in urban settings. Additionally, we believe that the principles derived from our analysis can be applied to a broader range of contexts involving the transmission of diseases in complex networks of interconnected components. In order to preserve the generality of the results, we avoid referencing any specific real-world application in the abstract. Nonetheless, the specific real-world application that inspired this research is mentioned in the concluding section of the paper. In this context, the findings of our study suggest that the adoption of fare payment systems that reduce bus transfers by up to 13% could effectively reduce the spread of illness on urban buses. The dissemination of information encouraging people to avoid busy buses also has the potential to reduce the spread of illness, although the efficacy of this approach is dependent on the level of awareness generated. The most suitable methodology for modeling the transmission of illnesses in confined settings, such as urban buses, involves the use of a well-mixed model that accounts for the exchange of individuals occurring at multiple scales. This type of model is particularly well-suited to modeling the transmission of illnesses in complex systems characterized by the flow of individuals across networks of interconnected components. In the context of urban buses, the probability of an individual becoming ill is directly proportional to the product of the average number of infected individuals and the duration of the bus trip, to the power of the number of individuals transferring between buses. Conversely, the probability of an individual remaining healthy is directly proportional to the product of the average number of non-infected individuals and the duration of the bus trip, to the power of the number of individuals transferring between buses. This mathematical concept is relevant to the study of material structures at the microscopic level. For a polyhedron to fully utilize available space with a high degree of precision, its geometric parameters must be precisely defined. Therefore, calculating a specific polyhedron volume using the general Eisenlohr-Farris formula may require additional constraints. This note also introduces a more constrained formula that can determine the volume of any selfsimilar, completely transitive polyhedron. This constrained formula utilizes the individual geometric parameters of the polyhedron's components. It enables the calculation of a specific polyhedron volume using its unique spatial orientation constraints. This is particularly useful in the study of microscopic material structures, where knowledge of a specific polyhedron's volume is essential. In contrast, this research introduces a novel, lightweight method for securing information exchange between sender and receiver in Gaussian noise environments. A fundamental property of these environments, known as the capacity-achieving property, can be leveraged to develop an unobtrusive and undetectable verification mechanism for the legitimate communication pair, without the need for shared secrets or keys. As a result, this new approach offers enhanced resilience to hardware tampering attacks and provides a level of security that is uncompromising and unyielding in the face of advancing technological capabilities. Furthermore, this new method employs a well-established and reliable metric called the probability of error to verify the authenticity of messages, rather than relying on vulnerable and easily compromised system information. In addition, this research showcases a pioneering application of physical communication systems as a means of securing information exchange, and highlights the unique advantages that this new method offers over conventional cryptographic techniques, such as the ability to securely transmit messages even when the communication device's software has been compromised, without compromising the efficiency of the system. The resulting external gas streams, referred to as a magnetosphere or a gust when referring to planetary conditions, can interact with their surrounding environment in several ways including absorbing incoming particles, diverting gas flow, and facilitating the detection of absorbed energy by re-emitting it in different forms. We introduce a novel approach to regularizing neural networks by imposing a consistent Lipschitz continuity constraint across all layers. Imposing this constraint directly is computationally impractical; instead, we develop an efficient and scalable optimization technique that leverages randomized testing to determine a neural network's Lipschitz constant and incorporates this into a consistent enforcement framework. This framework includes two primary methods for achieving consistent enforcement: one involves introducing a surrogates' enforcement term to the primary network's loss function, while another involves formulating consistent enforcement as a minimax optimization problem. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by achieving state-of-the-art accuracy in image classification tasks, notably surpassing the current best result in the CIFAR-10 dataset, as well as enhancing the robustness of neural networks in various scenarios. Moreover, our approach facilitates model interpretation by providing a measure of the diversity of features extracted by each layer. This diversity metric reveals that our method's enforcement of consistent layer behavior often results in extracted features that are less localized than those produced by traditional neural networks. We publicly release our code and a pre-trained model trained with our approach available at https://github.com/strmline/LCNR. Additionally, we provide an interactive visualization tool for feature maps extracted by our method and conventional neural networks at https://www.strmline.com/lcnr/. This enables visual comparison of our approach's results with those obtained from standard neural networks. Moreover, we introduce a publicly available PyTorch model that incorporates our innovative LCNR method, which achieves a top-of-the-line 94.37% accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset. This model serves as a prime example for researchers seeking to explore ways to enhance the robustness of neural networks. In rehabilitative games, models of optimal player performance can be used to measure progress and identify areas for improvement. By comparing a player's actual performance to expected performance under certain limitations, it becomes possible to tailor rehabilitation exercises to address specific needs. This concept is also applicable to broad applications involving decision-making under uncertainty. A mathematical framework can be applied to define a measure of a player's skill level and their strategy, while also accounting for any physical limitations that may affect their ability to execute actions. A simple rehabilitative exercise can be developed by utilizing an intuitive metric that indicates a player's ability to execute certain actions, such as executing a precise serve. A computational model can then be used to analyze a player's performance in a simulated environment, providing a clear framework for evaluating the effectiveness of rehabilitative games. A case study is presented, demonstrating the effectiveness of a rehabilitative exercise developed using this framework for a player with limited physical ability, and showing that it can identify areas of improvement that align with expert assessments. A key aspect of this research is the development of a formal definition for optimal baseline play, a concept previously described qualitatively in the rehabilitative games literature. A key contribution of this research is the development of a general framework for designing rehabilitative games, while also introducing a specific exercise that can be used to teach a fundamental skill in table tennis. A key limitation of this research is the use of a simplified model to analyze player performance, which may not accurately capture all aspects of their gameplay. The package lfda not only executes the LFDA algorithm but also offers post-processing functions to facilitate dimensionality reduction, visualization, and component analysis. The detailed execution procedure and a sample dataset are included within the documentation for easy access to the package's functionality. Moreover, the lfda package is readily available on CRAN. Additionally, the R package lfda includes a demonstration of its effectiveness in identifying cluster structures through dimensionality reduction. Furthermore, the lfda package also includes a demonstration of its capability in reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional data while retaining the original variability. In the context of social decision making, a serial dictatorship is a decision-making method where decisions are made by serving requests one at a time, with each user represented in a specific order. The issue of individual rank secrecy arises when some users may be unwilling to disclose their complete ranking of options, potentially hindering the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship approach. This problem is addressed by introducing a new method, called the "Proposed Procedure", which enables secure rank disclosure even with limited information, thereby enabling the utilization of serial dictatorships for sensitive information, thereby leveraging its proven efficiency and fairness. This new method is shown to be essentially equivalent to the original serial dictatorship method when all rank information is disclosed. Furthermore, the new method offers the same guaranteed social welfare and individual rank 2-strong monotonicity in cases where information is partially disclosed, thereby providing a way to incorporate user preferences in social decision making scenarios where trust and privacy are crucial concerns. This new method is applicable across a broad range of voting systems and can be seen as a new approach to addressing the issue of individual rank secrecy in social decision making. This research introduces two new concepts, called "strong monotonicity" and "rank k-strong monotonicity", which may have additional value in other contexts. This research is further supported by concrete examples and an associated formal model. No consensus exists on the origin of binary asteroids. One possible source could be the remnant of near-Earth asteroid collisions, whose size and frequency would be illuminated by studying their binary counterparts. To this end, researching binary asteroids among the NEA population is essential. Our team developed a new approach to detecting binary asteroids by utilizing the variation in light produced by the system as the two components orbit each other. This method involves utilizing the maximum and minimum brightness of the binary asteroid in relation to its orbit to factor in any light obstructed by the companion asteroid. By applying this approach to the Pan-STARRS1 database of asteroid observations, we were able to analyze 146 top candidates for binary asteroids, identifying 12 with an orbital period of less than 24 hours and 19 with an orbital period of 24 hours or more. Notably, we discovered the binary asteroid candidate 2019 AV6, with an orbital period of 12.377 hours, to have a significant light blockage indicating a substantial companion asteroid. This binary asteroid candidate 2019 AV6, with a diameter of approximately 280 meters, is the smallest NEA binary asteroid candidate with a confirmed period and light blockage, providing valuable insight for researchers. Furthermore, among all binary asteroid candidates discovered, only 2000 DK79 exhibited light blockage similar to that of 2019 AV6, and thus it is considered the most analogous to it. By incorporating physical properties derived from the taxonomic class of the main component of the asteroid 2019 AV6, our study suggests the mass of the companion asteroid to be approximately 0.164 kg, with a high likelihood of it being a similar, yet distinct object from the primary component. Consequently, the density of 2019 AV6 is estimated to be 1.68±0.31 times the density of Earth, classifying it as a type XH asteroid with a high metal content. Additionally, our study discovered the binary asteroid candidates 2019 AV6 and 2000 DK79 to possess a high probability of originating from a parent body with a high metal content, thus contributing valuable insight to the ongoing discussion about the formation of binary asteroid systems. Our study and the one conducted by the YORP effect driven binary asteroid candidates by Polishko and others, collectively shed new light on the vast population of the NEA binary asteroid population, and it is expected that a substantial portion of the NEA population will be comprised of objects similar to 2019 AV6. The model assumes that the partial effect of the network variables on the outcome can be described by a linear function, while the effect of other regressors is unspecified. We also examine the asymptotic behavior of the estimator, both under conditions of sparse and dense covariates. Located off the southern coast of Brazil, the Rio Grande Rise is an underwater volcanic plateau that formed as a result of massive volcanic activity during the Gondwanaland supercontinent's break-up. A vast, irregularly shaped ridge system, extending about 3,700 kilometers in length and 100-300 kilometers in width, characterizes this region. Studies using bathymetry and sub-bottom profiling have revealed the presence of numerous, elongated seamounts and volcanic edifices within the rise, which are aligned in a general NW-SE direction, parallel to the Atlantic coast. These features are part of the larger Rio Grande-Grand Banks volcanic ridge system, which formed as a result of the South Atlantic Ridge's southward movement over a fixed hotspot. As this volcanic axis has shifted due to the movement of the Atlantic Ocean's floor, a curved fissure has resulted, extending from the coast of Brazil to offshore of Bermuda. Studies using magnetic anomalies have dated the rise to the late Cretaceous period, around 118 million years ago. Observations from satellite altimetry have revealed the presence of a low-altitude dome in the center of the rise, which corresponds to areas of older volcanic rocks. This feature is distinct from the younger, more fractured volcanic edifices that make up the surrounding ridges. Data from gravity measurements in the air has allowed for an estimation of the density of rocks within the rise, which shows a higher density in the central dome, likely composed of basic rocks, compared to the surrounding areas, which are made up of more fractured and eroded acidic rocks. This variation in density may contribute to the unique shape of the dome within the rise. The volcanic rocks within the Rio Grande Rise have undergone significant alteration due to the interaction with seawater, particularly in areas where hydrothermal fluids have circulated, resulting in the precipitation of minerals such as manganese crusts and layers of hydrothermal sediment. These alterations have varying intensity, dependent on factors including the distance to the axis of the ridge, with increased circulation observed in areas further away from the axis. A prominent approach in medical image segmentation is information maximization, achieved through optimization of an image processing model, particularly notable is the method of contrastive learning, which has been successfully applied self-supervised medical image segmentation. This method involves two operations: a fully connected neural network is utilized to compare image feature vectors originating from different views, with the aim of separating them into similar and distinct groups according to whether the images are identical or different. Another approach involves two operations on the image boundary, namely, information maximization and mask estimation, which are both achievable via optimization of a neural network. This research introduces two innovative methods: one combines boundary-sensitive information maximization with mask estimation, leveraging a neural network to achieve both goals, and the other involves integrating self-supervised segmentation with mask estimation, both of which are shown to be effective in medical image segmentation. Notably, one of these methods uses a neural network to estimate the boundary of the target object, leading to a more accurate segmentation result compared to the baseline method, as demonstrated by the experimental results. This model enabled researchers to create an extensive database of knot types and their corresponding occurrences in proteins. By applying a topological analysis, they were able to create a diagram showing the relationships between different knot types and potential transition paths between them. This diagram reveals that some knot types are easily convertible, while others require more complex processes to transform from one to another. The latter group includes the trefoil-knot paired with a double trefoil knot, which is a non-classical knot structure found in only one protein out of ten million. For instance, the phrase "would have graduated" serves as a counterfactual to "did graduate". Although counterfactuals have been extensively studied in fields like psychology and philosophy, little research has been done on the construction of counterfactuals using phrasal structures - the focus of the proposed framework, DISCO. It demonstrates that fine-tuning these models on related tasks results in a significant improvement in their ability to create accurate counterfactuals. It further showcases that even without fine-tuning, contemporary language models exhibit a capacity to create some counterfactuals correctly, albeit with a limited understanding of the world. Nevertheless, the accuracy of these models in producing correct counterfactuals lags behind their baseline condition without any consideration of counterfactuals. The scope of this research is further narrowed down to focus exclusively on the production of factive counterfactuals. It incorporates an innovative method for evaluating the quality of generated counterfactuals and shows that the performance of DISCO surpasses that of the models producing basic descriptions. Lastly, it highlights the challenges associated with enhancing the ability of language models to create more sophisticated counterfactuals, particularly those described by the 'near' and 'far' framework proposed by Hansen et al. This research lays the groundwork for the exploration of multiple types of counterfactuals, including those that are not factive. It is anticipated that this study will contribute to the broader understanding of the relationship between the generation of counterfactuals and the generation of descriptive text. Furthermore, it is expected that the evaluation methods developed for this research will be applicable to the examination of other forms of counterfactuals. The development of models that can accurately create high-quality counterfactuals is likely to result in improvements in areas such as text classification, the generation of descriptive text, and the creation of narrative stories. The standard approach to constructing quantum theory within the categorical framework uses the global section functor from a presheaf category to Hilbert space. However, this method doesn't accommodate the category of unnormalizable states, which is essential for describing the universe of quantum mechanics. To resolve this issue, we've reworked the construction process, transforming the categorical theory into a equivalent formulation via category theory, specifically within the context of 2-categories. By doing so, we've established an equivalence between the category of unitary operators, unnormalizable states, and linear maps that preserve positivity, and the category of Hilbert space operators that preserve the unit status of status forms. This equivalence is then utilized to derive the unique operator corresponding to any physical observable or status form within the context of quantum theory. Furthermore, we've identified the category of normalizable states as an embedded subcategory within the broader context of quantum theory. These advancements provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between the fundamental structures of quantum theory and the categorical construction process. The resulting formulation enables the extraction of physical implications from categorically formulated theories, while also allowing the derivation of predictive implications for quantum theory. These insights can be applied across various formulations of quantum theory. The source of ultra-high-energy gamma-rays in nearby BL Lac objects, particularly those associated with large-scale jets, has remained a subject of debate for some time. To address this question, we must consider the magnetic properties of the jets. Using the Gravitational Lensing Effect to separate the host galaxy and the lens galaxy in the BGLE 0216+080 system, along with the use of radiogeneric templates to estimate the total luminosity of the jets, allows us to compare the electromagnetic spectra of the two lenses. As a result, we find that the fraction of electromagnetic energy carried by electrons in the jets is below 10%, indicating a significant presence of magnetic fields. In addition, we find that the strength of these magnetic fields is strong enough to dominate the electron-proton interaction, resulting in the dominance of electron-positron pairs over protons in the jet development, leading to the prediction of gamma-ray production through internal synchrotron radiation as the electrons move within the captured magnetic field of the jet. This theory not only explains the observed gamma-rays but also offers a more plausible explanation than the external Comptonized model, particularly in cases where the target photons are provided by the captured belts of the jets rather than host galaxies or accretion disks. Estimates of the gamma-ray luminosity and the electron energy distribution index provide valuable insights into the particle acceleration processes within these jets. Furthermore, our findings in BGLE 0216+080 also apply to Mrk 501, based on data obtained just before its giant flare in 2000, indicating a level of magnetic energy within the jet that is nearly double the energy required for the massive electron distribution responsible for the flare. This research underlines the significance of magnetic fields in high-energy gamma-ray production within these powerful jet systems. It also implies a level of energy that could result in the conversion of a significant portion of the jet kinetic energy into electromagnetic form, consistent with observations of numerous high-energy gamma-ray correlations with low-frequency radio flares in these systems. Additionally, the substantial presence of magnetic fields in these jets may significantly impact our understanding of their interaction with the surrounding environment, particularly in powerful engines such as supermassive black holes at the center of galaxies. It also highlights the importance of considering the capture of magnetic fields in jets when analyzing their behavior and the particle acceleration processes within them. This perspective may also provide a valuable insight into the functioning of other extreme high-energy particle accelerators found in the universe, such as binary systems, active galactic nuclei, and stellar jet

To illustrate this approach called 'feasible portfolio optimization,' we utilize two hypothetical investor groups with distinct risk preferences and use their combined preferences to map the risk-return spectrum. We then apply this method to actual data from the 2019 Zweig Report on Separate Accounts, employing two types of feasible portfolios: a uniform grid and a random sampling method. For complex biological processes monitored over time, a frequent task is to analyze and compare dynamic expression profiles from high-dimensional data sets, often involving the comparison of multiple sample groups or the assessment of gene expression profiles under varying conditions. Although machine learning techniques can simplify this process by identifying essential variables and distinctive temporal patterns from raw data, they often struggle with time series data that is concise and dimensionally high. A new technique has been developed to address this issue by using a combination of neural network guided learning and flexible spline-based modeling to accurately predict and compare temporal patterns in life science data sets. This technique requires fewer assumptions and is more robust to sample sizes and data dimensions than existing methods. It achieves this while minimizing the need for dimensionality reduction techniques that can sometimes obscure the underlying temporal patterns in the data. The effectiveness of this guided learning approach is demonstrated through its application to publicly available datasets of RNA expression profiles from time course experiments. It outperforms existing methods for guided learning and embedding of temporal data in multiple scenarios. The implementation of this technique in R is made available for public use. Additionally, a new dataset consisting of time series data from RNA expression profiles in Arabidopsis thaliana under various treatment conditions is also released for further research purposes. It comprises 11 different treatment conditions and includes 12 unique temporal patterns resulting from different types of cellular processes, such as gene regulation, metabolic pathways, and cell cycle processes. It can be downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus with the accession number GSE77343. Furthermore, an interactive visualization tool for comparing temporal patterns in life science data sets based on RNA expression profiles is introduced. It allows for the visualization of multiple temporal patterns in conjunction with the underlying data and is suitable for exploring and comparing temporal patterns in large datasets consisting of time series data from high-dimensional data sets. It is made available for public use and can be downloaded from the RStudio mirror closest to the user's location. Moreover, RStudio packages containing the implementation of this guided learning technique, the time series data from RNA expression profiles in Arabidopsis thaliana under various treatment conditions, and the interactive visualization tool for comparing temporal patterns in life science data sets are also available for public use. It is particularly designed for comparing temporal patterns in life science data sets from RNA expression profiles, gene regulation, metabolic pathways, and cell cycle processes under different conditions and processes. Human beings naturally possess the ability to accurately identify musical instruments even when they hear only a brief portion of a sound produced by those instruments. In contrast, developing computer systems capable of doing so across various categories of instruments poses a significant challenge. One critical obstacle is the vast disparity in sound patterns between different instruments, which can result in a high dimensional audio feature space. Another significant hurdle is the extensive array of musical instrument types available, which makes it difficult to conduct comprehensive training. To overcome these difficulties, a method has been proposed that uses a hierarchical framework to break down the task into two more manageable classification tasks: first, classifying sounds into categories of families (lacustrine, aerophonic, etc.), and then, classifying sounds into specific types (piano, guitar, etc.) within those families. By utilizing a hierarchical classifier and a prototype-based memory network in a meta-learning setting, our method successfully achieves accurate classification across 80 different types of musical instruments with only 10 training examples per class. Experimental results show that our proposed method surpasses existing methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MIR-1K dataset. The code for our method has been made publicly available on GitHub at the link provided. Furthermore, a preliminary evaluation of our method's performance on additional datasets is also included in the study. These results demonstrate that our proposed method consistently delivers superior performance across multiple datasets. To further validate the effectiveness of our method, an ablation study has been conducted which reveals that each component of the method plays a vital role in its success. In addition, the method's ability to handle a broad range of musical instrument types with rich auditory features has been demonstrated through additional experiments. The method's simplicity and the use of pre-trained models for both hierarchical classification and prototype-based memory network make it an efficient and highly scalable solution for musical instrument recognition in real-world applications. The method's potential applications in enhancing the usability of music players, improving sound effects in video games, and assisting musicians in identifying the instruments being played, among others, are also highlighted. In conclusion, the proposed method provides a scalable and efficient solution for musical instrument recognition in real-world scenarios and can be easily extended to classify other types of sounds such as animal voices, human voices, and natural environment sounds. Information-seeking questions pose an interesting problem for models, as they frequently mirror the format of formal definitions but with a distinct 'what does it mean?' flavor. Presently, numerous state-of-the-art models can generate definitions from scratch, yet the same cannot be said for answering these types of questions. Our initiative seeks to address this gap by creating a dataset comprised of 1,078 question and answer pairs, where each question stems from a formal definition found in Wikipedia, along with its corresponding answer rooted in research articles from arXiv. We outline various evaluation metrics for your models to assess the level of understanding they've gained from the dataset, involving both direct assessment approaches, reflecting on the clarity of the generated definitions, as well as more indirect indicators, such as the coherence of the produced summaries. Our benchmark model, albeit basic, has managed to achieve impressive results on the evaluation tests we devised, providing a solid foundation for future advancements in the domain of definition comprehension and formal concept learning. The underlying dataset we created, although concentrated on mathematical concepts, can serve as a starting point for the exploration of a broader range of domains and subject matters. Typically, a Majorana fermion is represented by a 2N-dimensional matrix representation, which we reduce to a linear form in this case (denoted as L-Majorana). This particle exhibits distinct behavior under continuous Hermitian basis transformations. Due to the linearity of its defining equation, the L-Majorana wavefunction displays invariance under a specific transformation, resulting in the disappearance of certain interference terms in its probability distribution. As a result, the L-Majorana particle's behavior is described by a mixture of continuous Gaussian and Beta-distributed variables. We also derive the conditions under which the L-Majorana particle's behavior mimics that of a standard fermionic particle. In our previous research on binary data storage using DNA, we identified the slow update feature of DNA storage as a major performance limitation. This bottleneck occurs because once DNA strands are written, the same nucleotide base cannot be used again in the same storage unit. This constraint forces an unnecessary data duplication when attempting to update already stored binary data, a necessary operation in many applications. To overcome this limitation, we first discovered a way to represent binary data using DNA with a more flexible update characteristic. Building on this, we created an efficient update algorithm that minimizes the number of nucleotide base replications. To further optimize updates, we examined various hierarchy designs and pinpointed a specific structure that achieves optimal update performance while maintaining decent query performance. Finally, a method we devised allows for seamless integration of updated DNA data with other storage units, solving yet another update-related challenge. As a result, our research offers an effective solution to efficiently achieve both updates and query operations on DNA storage. This storage technology is particularly suitable for applications that involve a large amount of diverse data with occasional updates and queries. In our implementation, we achieved significant performance improvements, reducing the time it takes to update large datasets by a factor of 100 or more. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, radiologists face difficulties in this task due to the irregular shape of tumors and the presence of different tumor types in MRI images.  This paper introduces a Multi-task focus directed network called MAG-Net, which is designed to address these challenges by allowing the focus of tumor types to be adjusted.  Experiments using the BRATS 2019 dataset showed MAG-Net to outperform existing models, achieving a high Dice similarity coefficient of 0.809, 0.867, and 0.829 for whole tumor, tumor core, and enhancement segments, respectively, and a classification accuracy of 0.814 for tumor types.  Furthermore, a reduced-parameter variant of MAG-Net demonstrated competitive performance to the full model, indicating potential applications in low-resource settings.  The code for MAG-Net has been made available on the GitHub platform.  Future directions for improving MRI-based tumor diagnosis include the exploration of lightweight models and multi-task learning techniques.  By integrating spatial and chromatic information from MRI images, future work aims to develop more effective tumor segmentation and classification networks.  The proposed MAG-Net model has the potential to contribute to such research.  The use of focus directed modules in MAG-Net has shown improved performance on the BRATS dataset, which could also be applicable to other medical image analysis tasks.  The focus directed module can be trained end-to-end with a segmentation decoder, enabling flexible application to various medical image datasets.  The proposed MAG-Net model has multiple applications in medical imaging diagnostics, including the automatic detection of tumors and better treatment planning.  By enhancing the accuracy of tumor segmentation and classification, MAG-Net has the potential to contribute to these efforts.  The improved performance of MAG-Net on the BRATS dataset makes it a more effective tool for tumor diagnosis than previous models.  The focus directed module can be adapted for use with other medical image datasets, such as the ISBI 2019 dataset.  The proposed MAG-Net model can be adapted for use with these datasets, or variations of them, such as the BRATS 2020 dataset.  The use of a reduced-parameter variant of MAG-Net has shown that the model can be applied to low-resource settings.  The code for the proposed MAG-Net model has been made available on the GitHub platform.

Reconstructing an scene from an image is a key problem in computer vision, especially when using images containing cast shadows.  The presence of these shadows can severely impede the image processing algorithms used for subsequent tasks, as they mislead the algorithms about the true geometry of the scene.  Traditionally, removing shadows has been a prerequisite for accurately computing the scene's geometry, a task that has been a major obstacle in the field's progress. Our novel approach overcomes this challenge.  We've developed a differentiable shadow detection and removal method that allows shadow-casted areas to be identified and the effects of shadows removed during the reconstruction of the scene.  This achieved through a convenient integration of our shadow detection module with the existing differentiable reconstruction framework.  By utilizing our module's output along with the reconstructed scene's pixels, a new objective function can be defined that combines the performance of both the shadow detection and the scene's reconstruction.  Our results, obtained using deep learning-based architectures for both the shadow detection and the scene's reconstruction, demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in accurately detecting and removing shadows, as well as enhancing the output of the scene's reconstruction.  This is exemplified through the accurate reconstruction of characters from images containing cast shadows. Our method's code is available for public use at https://github.com/wangy86/ShadowDifferentiable. Machine learning experts frequently leverage neural network-based their own variations in a top-down manner, often incorporating multiple layers of a standard neural network. Understanding the underlying structure of these complex models is, therefore, crucial. Our analysis reveals a causal framework that is applicable across various configurations of neural networks, including multi-layer perceptrons, convolutional neural networks, and recurrent neural networks. This framework enables the interpretation of each layer in the network by explaining its output and the subsequent layer's subsequent input. The rise of safety-aware deep learning algorithms through robust optimization techniques has led to a surge in research focused on their effectiveness. Unfortunately, the development of methods evaluating the security of neural networks has outpaced the development of methods enhancing security. As a result, it has become essential to scrutinize the credibility of neural networks constructed using current deep learning practices. In this research, an open-ended survey was conducted among seasoned deep learning researchers, and the responses received were thoroughly analyzed in an effort to gain insight into the perceptions of these experts regarding the safety of neural networks. The findings indicate that, according to these researchers, the current state-of-the-art neural networks are reliable in specific situations but are vulnerable to deception, and as such, evaluating the validity of a neural network requires considering more than just its accuracy. In fact, the responses revealed that approximately 75% of those surveyed believed their recently trained neural networks were secure, yet a substantial proportion of them acknowledged that these networks were prone to deception. In light of these findings, the concept of "safety" is redefined to encompass not only the resistance of a neural network to being deceived but also its overall dependability. In this context, the term "deceptive safety" refers to a neural network's ability to accurately present misleading information as factual. In order to further investigate this concept, a straightforward yet rigorous framework is introduced that assesses the deceptive safety of a neural network based on its ability to generate convincing, misleading class predictions on a test dataset. In addition, a novel metric is introduced that evaluates the diverse range of misleading class predictions generated by a neural network. In order to evaluate the efficacy of this framework, a comprehensive evaluation of the deceptive safety of neural networks was conducted, and the results revealed that the current state-of-the-art deep learning models exhibit varying levels of deceptive safety, with some models exhibiting a high degree of unsafe behavior. In order to mitigate this unsafe behavior, a new training algorithm was developed that achieves superior performance in comparison to existing training algorithms, and the improvements gained are substantial when the model is large. In particular, the new algorithm was found to effectively minimize the dense region of misleading class predictions in the probability space, thereby enhancing the overall performance. In conclusion, the findings of this research underscore the importance of scrutinizing the credibility of neural networks in a holistic manner, and the novel algorithm developed offers a solution to the complex problem of mitigating the deceptive safety of neural networks through optimized model training. In light of these discoveries, the stage is set for a deeper exploration of the subject matter

A fundamental theory is presented that applies to both linear and Kerr nonlinear resonators and waveguides, enabling a unified explanation for the unique properties and behavior exhibited under both coherent and incoherent driving conditions. The theory offers a novel mathematical framework that transforms any linear mode or a Schrödinger equation with a nonlinear Kerr term into an equivalent effective linear problem. This results in the emergence of discrete symmetries in vacuum optical resonators, regardless of the geometric parameters. The novel approach also facilitates the analysis of coupled resonators or waveguides, revealing new transformation and dimer symmetry properties that affect the mode coupling and nonlinear phenomena, such as four-wave mixing. Furthermore, the theory demonstrates that coherent (laser) operation is governed by the same rules as in vacuum resonators, while incoherent (semiclassical) operation is affected by mode competition, with a universal mode-competition coefficient determined by the resonator's geometric parameters. The theory offers a practical solution to the complex problem of finding the resonator's eigenmodes and their linear and nonlinear coupling dynamics. It provides an analytical expression for the mode-competition coefficient, allowing for the prediction of incoherent dynamics without the need for numerical calculations. The theory is applicable to any type of resonator or waveguide, regardless of its geometric parameters, and enables the design of resonators with optimized performance. The approach can further be extended to multimer systems, and the theory is also relevant to metasurfaces, providing insights to optimize their performance. The novel theory offers a breakthrough in the understanding of linear and nonlinear optical resonator and waveguide dynamics, enabling the development of high-performance sources of light, as well as various optical operations, such as lasing, four-wave mixing, and the generation of light-frequency up- and down-converted from a coherent drive. The theory can be used to design resonators and waveguides with reduced mode competition, a crucial component for the development of resonant quantum chemistry in the macroscopic domain. The approach provides a pathway to the realization of complex multimer quantum chemistry experiments in the macroscopic domain, as well as the fabrication of unique optical metamaterials with customized properties. The theory can also be applied to waveguides filled with nonlinear metamaterials, enabling the development of new light-sources and optical devices. The novel approach resolves the long-standing challenge of achieving resonant quantum chemistry in the macroscopic domain, as well as resolves the outstanding issue of developing high-performance light-sources based on resonator and waveguides.

Reinforcement learning agents that can adapt to an endless stream of tasks, or the same tasks with varying parameters, are needed. This paper introduces the concept of lifelong reinforcement learning, which involves learning across an infinite series of related tasks. We also present a unified framework for evaluating the performance of lifelong reinforcement learning agents in a variety of scenarios, including learning multiple independent tasks and learning across scenarios with interdependent episodes. This evaluation framework is realized through a minimalistic 2D exploration scenario, called the Gridworld 2D, which allows for various configuration options to capture the essence of real-world applications. The characteristics of this environment ensure that any successful lifelong reinforcement learning method evaluated on Gridworld 2D will likely succeed in adapting to complex scenarios as well. The code for the environment and a basic lifelong reinforcement learning agent has been made publicly available. By standardizing the evaluation procedures and the architecture of the evaluation environment, the performance of different lifelong reinforcement learning agents can be fairly and comprehensively compared. Furthermore, our approach is also applicable to other domains that involve reasoning about dynamic processes and effects. Despite its effectiveness, the category system's ability to learn from multi-class data has not been thoroughly explored, mainly because the current CSSVD methodology does not adequately account for data that can categorize itself as incorrect. To address this limitation, a new method for data with self-devaluation is proposed, which enables the category system to refine its predictions through self-cancellation. By integrating this approach into CSSVD, a new algorithm called Self-Invalidation and Self-Devaluation Category System (SISCSD) is developed, allowing the category system to learn from multi-class data with self-invalidations and self-devaluations. Through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, SISCSD is shown to outperform the current CSSVD baseline across multiple benchmark datasets. Furthermore, SISCSD's effectiveness is demonstrated across various graph machine learning models, including node classification, graph classification, and molecular property prediction. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with most proposed relationships being incorrect but easily recognizable. This leads to a situation where the model easily classifies these easy positive proposals as correct, but cannot distinguish them from similar negative proposals. As a result, the model becomes overconfident in its predictions and focuses on these easy positives rather than challenging ones. To address this issue, we proposed two main contributions. Firstly, we introduced a balanced proposal distribution by incorporating a proposal filtering mechanism based on model confidence. This filters out easy positive proposals and reduces the number of proposed relationships by half. Secondly, we designed an inter-instance conflict mechanism to encourage the model to select more challenging positive proposals. During testing, we employed an adaptive proposal filtering mechanism to strike a balance between precision and recall. FPGA), a novel computing paradigm. Each point in the grid of the FPGA is equipped
with an identical, independent processing unit that can be programmably linked,
allowing for the efficient realization of custom, highly performant systems by
leveraging hundreds of tiny processing cores. The unique feature of this architecture
is the ability to directly map data structures, addresses, and associated procedures
onto the FPGA grid, enabling seamless data processing and reducing the need for
explicit memory management. Furthermore, the inclusion of a built-in safety mechanism
prevents write access to areas of the grid that do not contain program code, thereby
eliminating the risk of memory safety errors and related system crashes. A concrete
implementation of this concept is also presented, where each APC unit is designed
as a simple RISC-style processor that supports loading, execution of instructions,
and basic operation management. Additionally, a demonstration of a custom system
built using the APC framework is presented, showcasing how the unique features of
this architecture can be utilized to develop both efficient and reliable systems. The
efficiency of this architecture is attributed to the tight integration of processing
cores with data structures and processing code, a characteristic that is inherently
compatible with the spirit of the Data-Oriented Design paradigm. Furthermore, the
memory safety errors that can arise from incorrect use of pointers are avoided in this
architecture, a type of programming error that is notoriously difficult to detect
and fix but can be avoided altogether in programs built using the APC framework. The
performance and reliability of this architecture make it an attractive option for
developing systems that require low-latency, real-time operation. The unique features

Due to the extensive parameters involved, determining the GS0F model parameters remains a challenging task. A more viable method involves Monte Carlo simulations to sample the likelihood function, thereby allowing for an exploration of the parameter space. In quantum computing, measuring mid-circuits can cause significant problems, including steering the circuit into an undesired state or diminishing the circuit's final outcome. This challenge has prompted the development of quantum circuits with reconfigurable measurements, allowing the re-setting of mid-circuit measurements without needing actual re-execution. Despite such advancements, identifying the specific measurements that are causing issues during mid-circuits remains a problem. This paper introduces a novel approach, called idenQMAD, which automatically pinpoints problematic measurement acts in mid-circuit quantum applications. idenQMAD achieves this by comparing a circuit's behavior with different measurement bases, using a distinct quantum circuit for identifying anomalies, until a specific fault is found, with a time complexity of $O(\sqrt{n})$ for circuits of $n$ quantum gates. Additionally, idenQMAD can locate all instances of measurement anomalies in $O(n)$ time, making it an extremely efficient and practical solution for a wide range of quantum applications. This includes various forms of quantum simulation, homogenous linear differential equation solving, and cryptographic protocols like port-based encryption and secret sharing. Furthermore, idenQMAD incorporates a unique, post-processing technique called clean-up, which transforms an identifying circuit into an equivalent equivalent one that has a reduced depth, thus further enhancing its performance. This includes the creation of compact, portable quantum applications, such as the development of quantum protocols for solving certain system of linear equations, homogeneous and non-homogeneous. The source code for idenQMAD has been made publicly available on an open-source repository, demonstrating its practical utility and effectiveness. In particular, our experiments using a full-scale simulator on real-world datasets, such as the HHL96, port-based encryption, and a system of linear equations with $128$ variables, show that idenQMAD outperforms a proposed alternative solution, QMA-Identify, by an order of magnitude in terms of execution time. For instance, idenQMAD successfully identifies all measurement anomalies in the HHL96 in approximately $580$ microseconds, whereas QMA-Identify takes roughly $6.73$ seconds on the same dataset. This research aims to examine whether such methods can yield comparable results for more general CSPs representing various graph properties.

Using an extended version of the SH-LDPC framework that accommodates additional CSP forms, such as Maximum Cut or Minimum Edge Cover, this study proves the existence of a PTAS for a broad class of CSPs, including those that capture properties like independent sets in different types of graphs.

However, the paper also identifies restrictions that prevent the application of standard LDPC structures, such as the presence of specific negative instances in some graph classes.

Furthermore, even when such data is available, it is often insufficient to train models for multiple tasks simultaneously. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In a previous study, it was demonstrated how these conditions could be met by incorporating a form of anti-monadic typing into the language. Yet, implementing this approach within the GP 2 compiler proved intricate, resulting in a cumbersome compiler architecture that hindered the development of efficient GP 2 programs. This research presents an enhanced version of the GP 2 compiler, streamlining the compiler architecture while retaining the benefits of the original's efficient rule matching functionality. The improved compiler utilizes a more manageable compiler architecture called two-stage compilation, achieved by reconfiguring the compiler's intermediate representation and its optimization phases. This revised compiler architecture facilitates straightforward program transformations, such as the addition of performance-oriented compiler intrinsics, thereby enabling the development of efficient GP 2 programs. We uncover an infinite lineup of star normal quotient graphs that are derived from twisted wreath structures, a significant infinite class of star normal quotient graphs that cannot be categorized under the banners of twisted graphs or star normal quotient graphs associated with wreath structures. Additionally, within this line-up, we identify a subgroup whose generators' pair lengths correlate directly with the size of the base set within the twisted wreath structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spectral pattern of these star normal quotient graphs, when ordered chronologically, conforms to the pattern identified by Rowland, specifically within the broad spectral range $\Lambda-\sqrt{\Lambda}$, where $\Lambda$ represents the maximal eigenvalue. Our research also highlights the presence of an invariant, referred to as the twisted wreath invariant, that differentiates these star normal quotient graphs from their counterparts within the twisted graph class. Our work is further substantiated by illustrations and computations presented in the appendices. 
Firstly, our findings provide a general formula for deriving the eigenvalues of these star normal quotient graphs through the use of the twisted wreath invariant.
Secondly, our research includes an examination of the grid-like structures that underlie these star normal quotient graphs, revealing their equivalence to specific arrangements of complete graphs, as well as certain hypercubes and cubic circulant graphs.

Our research utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies (U/LIRGs) within a distance of 180 Mpc, all located at a redshift of less than 0.04. The spectra we collected with a spatial resolution of 750-850 pc and an emission line velocity resolution of approximately 300 km/s, allowed us to analyze various gas dynamics including outflows, recurrent interactions, and gas motions associated with death stars. Our data include high-ionization lines such as HeII$\lambda$4686, CIII$\lambda$5150, and CIV$\lambda$5643, which demonstrate high-ionization states in the nuclei of 5 galaxies (55%), as well as several galaxies (22%) exhibiting signs of ionized gas outflows in multiple areas. Our findings also reveal the presence of double-ionized gas outflows in 33% of the galaxies and show that the majority (67%) of U/LIRGs exhibit star formation rates higher than 10% of their galaxy mass formation rates. These results demonstrate the capability of the KOOLS-IFU to obtain optical IFU data on target galaxies and highlight the potential of such data to identify the numerous hidden death stars that are forming massive stars and contributing to the outflows seen in U/LIRGs. Lastly, our research highlights the versatility of the KOOLS-IFU as an optical IFU system that can obtain a wide range of target galaxy data, from nearby U/LIRGs to distant active galactic nuclei.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially introduced with eight separate disk modules, the upgraded version features 100% coverage courtesy of three closely aligned disks, comprised of 48 individual modules. However, the increased readout volume and reduced signal-to-noise ratio pose significant processing challenges. To mitigate these issues, the implementation of an analog zero-suppression technique known as the "edge cluster" method has been developed and tested using data from the upgraded pilot modules. Compared to traditional digital techniques, this approach demonstrates a marked increase in accepted hits by 20-30%, enabling a 5-6 times greater equivalent gain before overwhelming noise for a given digital configuration. Furthermore, this strategy facilitates a 1-2 times greater acceptance of valid hits at the same digital threshold. As a result, the need for higher digital thresholds is obviated, thereby offsetting the required increase in data bandwidth for the upgraded CMS pixel detector. Additionally, the challenge of digital threshold setting is diminished to a minimum. Moreover, the improved performance of this technique is attributed to a more refined algorithm for determining the cluster edge, showcasing the effectiveness of simulation in predicting the outcome, thus allowing for suitable design choices. It is known that p_n is submultiplicative and satisfies the inequality p_(nk) \geq (p_n)^k for any positive integer k. We aim to analyze the nontrivial recurrence threshold, defined as the supremum of all p_n such that p_n^k is less than 1 for any k. By demonstrating that the sequence p_n^k accumulates to 0 for almost all values of p_n below this supremum, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the essential density, denoted as \lambda. Furthermore, we prove that the supremum of the irrationals within the range (0, 1) consists of two components: the highest component is the greatest pure action within a k-ary tree, and the lowest component is the highest component of the pure actions within trees of arbitrary degree. Consequently, the density of survival probabilities for the frog model on a k-ary tree is equal to the highest pure action within a k-ary tree for any positive integer k. In 3D medical image analysis, using whole networks for feature extraction can be ineffectual if the network is poorly trained on limited or low-quality data, leading to unsatisfactory diagnostic results. This issue is particularly pronounced due to the vast amount of parameter options in 3D feature extractors relative to their 2D counterparts. To circumvent this problem, we propose an innovative hybrid approach, combining 2D feature extraction with 3D edge-based information integration. This approach leverages the expertise of both 2D feature extractors and 3D edge detectors to enhance the accuracy of semantic segmentation in medical images, even in scenarios with limited, noisy, or incomplete data. We demonstrate the superiority of our method by applying it to the MHI-AD dataset, a widely used dataset for Alzheimer's disease analysis, and showcasing its superior performance relative to multiple baseline approaches in experiments conducted on multiple variants of the dataset. Notably, our method achieved a notable increase in Dice coefficient values of up to 9.5% when compared to the standard 3D CNN baseline. The enhanced performance of our method is attributed to its ability to mitigate the over-extraction of noisy cues typical of deep learning-based 3D feature extractors. We further analyze the results by graphically visualizing the 3D feature maps extracted using our edge-gated CNNs, illustrating their ability to suppress the extraction of unnecessary spatial cues. This, in turn, enables accurate semantic segmentation even in scenarios with limited, noisy, or incomplete data. Furthermore, we highlight the versatility of our method by applying it to various medical image analysis tasks, including multi-organ segmentation and abnormality detection. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide an open-source implementation of our approach, referred to as Edge-Gated 3D CNNs. This code is publicly available for download at https://github.com/seyedmohammadghasemi/EdgeGated3D-CNNs. Additionally, we have included a detailed guide on modifying the code to adapt our method for use in (1) multi-organ segmentation and (2) abnormality detection. Moreover, to facilitate the sharing of research resources, we have created an open-access dataset repository called the Medical Image Analysis Baseline Models and Algorithms Repository (https://github.com/seyedmohammadghasemi/Medical-Image-Analysis-Baselines). This repository encompasses an extensive collection of open-access medical datasets and provides a comprehensive platform for evaluating and comparing the performance of various image analysis algorithms

MongoDB, a popular NoSQL database, employs transactional operations to maintain data consistency.  Given the complexity of MongoDB's document-based storage, ensuring transactional integrity across all documents within a sharded cluster is a significant challenge.  To effectively validate the integrity of MongoDB transactions, a systematic approach is necessary to address the inherent differences between document and unit storage.

  Previously proposed methods for validating transactions are limited to single-node configurations and existing integrity checking approaches for MongoDB have not considered a sharded environment.  Furthermore, none of these methods facilitate the correction of failed transactions or the detection of partial updates.

  To address these limitations, we introduce an original method for validating MongoDB transactions within a sharded cluster.  Our approach not only identifies failed transactions but also provides the necessary update commands to correct them.  Additionally, we have developed a prototype of our method and conducted extensive testing on a MongoDB document sharding cluster.

  The testing involved over 100,000 unit operations and 15,000 transactional operations in a shared cluster configuration.  The testing used the YCSB and OLTPBench performance evaluation tools and showed that the overhead of using our method is minimal.  Specifically, the results showed that the overhead of using our method for single-node configuration is 1.16% for read-intensive workloads and 11.08% for update-intensive workloads.  In a multi-node configuration the overhead is 4.42% for read-intensive workloads and 12.82% for update-intensive workloads.  The testing also showed that the time it takes to validate all units within a transactional batch is 25.19 milliseconds on average.  The testing used a MongoDB cluster with four shard nodes and one confict resolution node.  The testing used a Intel Xeon E5-2697v3 CPU with 16 cores and 64GB of RAM in each node. The testing used a MongoDB cluster with a memory of 64GB and a storage of 1TB in each node. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. Notably, this work differs from standard malicious attack models, which assume attackers directly manipulate the objective function, rather than requiring significant larger steps. Instead, the proposed algorithm assumes attackers can influence the variable updates through false information, affecting optimization variability. This model is particularly relevant to applications with multi-agent connections, such as smart grids and wireless sensor networks.
