Our primary acoustic localization technique, based on inter-aural time differences (ITD) and inter-aural level differences (ILD), is effective in most situations but fails for certain frequency-independent sounds. These sounds have minimal or no ITD and ILD, often because they lack binaural components or consistent periodic patterns. Examples include crackling, rustling, and clicking sounds. Our challenge lies in developing a method to localize these difficult sounds through a process that involves learning sound features from a variety of sources, including auditory simulations, actual sounds, and noise. Our system uses a deep learning technique called a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN) to determine a universal sound representation that can localize all sounds, including the hard ones. This representation is unique to the audio domain and does not rely on visual information. We trained our model on a diverse dataset containing 1,000 sounds and found that it could localize sounds with an error of less than 22 degrees in all directions. This technique has the potential to enhance the localization of difficult sounds in various applications and could potentially be incorporated into virtual reality and mixed reality technologies. Additionally, our model can be used to create artificial sounds that are similar to real sounds, a capability that could be useful in creating customizable sound effects and realistic game sounds. This involves using a part of the CGAN called a generator to create artificial binaural sound recordings based on a given sound class. Our results show that our model can create realistic sounds with a accuracy of over 80%. This technique and our results demonstrate the potential of deep learning to solve complex acoustic localization challenges. Furthermore, our method can be used to create a more comprehensive sound dataset that includes both real and artificially generated sounds. This dataset includes over 10,000 sounds generated from 400 different classes, such as animal sounds, human actions, and natural environments. This dataset can be used to train more robust sound classification and detection models. Our approach and our results also demonstrate the value of using both actual sound recordings and auditory simulations to train a sound localization model. This is because actual sound recordings provide the model with the unique characteristics of actual sounds, such as their frequency content and duration, while auditory simulations enable the model to focus on the intrinsic features of sound that are essential for localization, such as their pitch, rhythm, and binaural components. This combined approach results in a model that can accurately localize all types of sounds, including the hard ones, and has a wide range of applications in various fields, including audio processing, virtual reality

Multi-layer graph neural networks (GNNs) have effectively been applied to social influence analysis, information diffusion, and other processes that follow the spread of relationships. However, most existing GNN models are based on an Eulerian approach and neglect the direction of network connections, which can lead to inaccurate results when the network is asymmetric. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel type of neural network called the Lorentzian GNN, which takes into account the direction of network connections. By incorporating a new form of neighbor aggregation that is based on the Lorentzian distance, this model is able to preserve the graph structure in a non-Eulerian manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the Lorentzian GNN by evaluating its performance on multiple benchmark datasets for link prediction, node classification, and influence maximization. Our results indicate that the Lorentzian GNN outperforms state-of-the-art GNN models on most tasks, suggesting its potential as a more comprehensive and effective approach for modeling complex network processes. Our implementation is also highly efficient, with a high degree of model parallelism that enables the training of large graphs. Furthermore, the Lorentzian GNN is a flexible model that can be readily integrated with additional graph embedding methods to enhance its performance. By incorporating the direction of network connections, the Lorentzian GNN provides a more precise and accurate representation of the graph, which is critical in applications that rely heavily on network structures. Our results highlight the advantages of the Lorentzian GNN over traditional GNN models, which fail to consider the direction of network connections. By acknowledging the orientation of graph connections, the Lorentzian GNN is better suited for graphs with bi-directional edges, providing a more comprehensive and effective approach for modeling complex network processes. Our implementation of the Lorentzian GNN is a high-performance model that includes a dynamic reduction trick and a batch normalization layer, enabling its successful application to large graphs. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of the Lorentzian GNN by evaluating its performance on multiple benchmark datasets for link prediction, node classification, and influence maximization, with results indicating that the model outperforms state-of-the-art GNN models on most tasks. Our results also highlight the potential of the Lorentzian GNN to accurately capture the graph structure in a non-Eulerian manner, providing a more precise and accurate representation of the graph. Our research on the Lorentzian GNN has far-reaching implications for the study of complex network processes

A key challenge in applied mathematics involves solving the reverse problem, which entails determining an unknown physical parameter based on observable fluid dynamics. In this context, we explore the scenario of an acoustic wave interacting with a rigid body. The underlying physics is governed by the Helmholtz equation and the Kirchhoff plate equation. By formulating the reverse problem as an operator equation, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for it to be well-defined and uniquely solvable. Furthermore, we develop a numerical technique to approximate the unknown boundary condition, utilizing the Discontinuous Galerkin method in combination with the Nitsche penalty approach. This method facilitates the use of high-order approximations and imposes consistent essential boundary conditions. Additionally, we implement an iterative fixed point method to solve the reverse problem, leveraging the weak admissibility of the Diophantine operator. A notable advantage of this approach is that it preserves the regularity of the target boundary condition. The accuracy of this numerical technique is verified through a series of test cases, including scenarios with periodic boundary conditions and an oscillating plate. The former leads to the existence of non-trivial solutions, while the latter results in a unique solution. The proposed method also handles cases with distinct frequencies. The numerical results demonstrate a direct relationship between the number of degrees of freedom and the inverse of the condition number of the system matrix, with the error exhibiting an almost linear increase. The method has the advantage of using the same mesh and time step size for both the forward and reverse problems, and the computational cost is proportional to the square of the number of degrees of freedom. The method is highly efficient, with a significant reduction in the degree of freedom required to achieve a certain level of error in comparison to the existing literature. The implementation of an optimal control problem formulation has been initially explored, but a more in-depth analysis of this variant of the reverse problem remains a subject for future research. The code developed in this study has been successfully ported to a GPU, with the numerical results showing a significant speedup of up to 5.5 times when using a single GPU, and an additional speedup of up to 4 times when using multiple GPUs. The proposed method has numerous potential applications and could be adapted to other types of acoustic wave equations. The notion of negative absolute temperature, initially met with skepticism, has been consistently supported by theoretical models and a substantial number of experimental results. In this presentation, we will begin by explaining the conceptual framework of negative absolute temperature, including a discussion on the Bianchi identity that some argue is the true temperature definition. We then move on to examining the various methods for achieving negative absolute temperatures, whether through optical techniques, atomic and molecular setups, or even macroscopic devices, and discuss the inherent relationships between them. Furthermore, we investigate the fundamental applications of negative absolute temperatures in both thermal and non-thermal equilibrium scenarios, and explore the broader implications for our understanding of temperature and its connections to other physical concepts. Finally, we offer a glimpse into the exciting possibilities that the study of negative absolute temperatures may unlock in the future. Editors: S. Manchanda, A. M. Ignat'ev. Organizers: S. Manchanda, A. M. Ignat'ev. Chair: A. M. Ignat'ev. This talk is based on section II, III, IV and V of the review article: "Negative absolute temperature: Theory, experiments and applications" arXiv:1905.02444v2, published in 2020. Due to time constraints, discussion on equations and some recent developments will be skipped. Nonetheless, the talk is intended to provide an overview of the topic in question and is thus suitable for a young audience with limited background knowledge. In the interest of clarity, some complex concepts will be defined within the talk, and to facilitate further understanding, a list of key terms used is included at the end. This includes definitions for antitransport, heat pump, engines, cooling systems, Coherent Population Oscillations, Counter-Abundance, CPB, DC current, HEWB, IWB, Josephson junction, Larmor precession, LC circuit, Luttinger liquid, quantum dot, SQUID, and two-component mixture. Full definitions can be found in the supplied bibliography. At the outset, I would like to express gratitude to my collaborator, Dr. S. Manchanda, for his invaluable insights and contributions. In addition, I would like to extend heartfelt appreciation to my wife, Dr. A. M. Ignat'ev, for her unwavering support throughout this research. On a lighter note, I would like to joke that my wife is the reason I am aware of negative absolute temperatures in the first place. In the interest of full disclosure

Characterizing colorectal polyps histology involves a comprehensive evaluation of a sample's cellular structure for both form and function, involving intricate insights into the tissue's architecture and the abnormal cell growth within. This complex process is crucial for identifying malignant potential but is complicated by the variability in tissue samples and subjective interpretation of dysplastic signs. To tackle this challenge, researchers need large, high-quality datasets with precise annotations to support both deep learning-based image analysis and traditional approaches. In response, our institution's department of pathologic anatomy collaborated to create the UniToPatho dataset, comprising 8286 annotated sections obtained from whole-slide images of colorectal polyps, collected from multiple sources and diverse in their level of neoplastic cell growth. These annotations detail the presence or absence of specific features related to structure and cell growth within the tissue sample. Furthermore, a robust dataset evaluation was designed to assess the performance of deep learning-based classification models, and our results show that a relatively small number of samples can support the development of efficient, dysplasia-grading models. To facilitate further research, UniToPatho is made available for public access and contribution under an open-source framework. By uniting efforts in image annotation, model development, and research, we hope to create a comprehensive framework for addressing challenges in whole-slide image analysis and a platform for exploring solutions to other complex problems in this field. UniToPatho's code for image preprocessing, a dataset extension policy, and a evaluation tool can be found at https://github.com/unito-ibaw/UniToPatho, and the dataset itself is accessible via https://ibaw.unito.it/datasets/unito-pathology. By building upon this initiative, we invite all researchers and practitioners to collaborate and contribute to the advancement of whole-slide image analysis. Our experience developing UniToPatho highlights the benefits of collaborating with an institution's department of pathologic anatomy and underscores the importance of open-source data extension policies, which we believe will yield valuable insights for similar multidisciplinary projects. By combining strengths in both fields, we can create high-quality datasets that facilitate the advancement of whole-slide image analysis and a collaborative framework for addressing other related challenges. UniToPatho has been recognized as a distinguished dataset in the field of whole-slide image analysis and has received the distinction "Certificate of Merit" at MICCAI 2020 in the category of Datasets. Isotopic analysis indicated a higher deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio in the pyroxene minerals (648±129 times the natural standard) compared to similar minerals from older falls of the Lossers and Bisei meteorites (23±8 times the natural standard). This significant difference suggests that planetesimals in the inner solar system experienced moisture accumulation during the assembly of the solar system and supports previous findings from the analysis of meteorites from the CM chondrite group. Furthermore, this discovery provides evidence for the preservation of water isotopic signals in terrestrial planets through multiple stages of planetary differentiation and core formation. It also offers a greater understanding of how water isotopes vary across the inner solar system. Speech translation combines speech recognition and machine translation to enable
language interpretation for those who cannot communicate effectively due to
language barriers. Advanced systems have achieved substantial progress in various
settings, including systems that can translate speech independently, remove
background noise, and handle multi-speaker environments. However, current systems
require the same medium for input and output - for example, speech to speech,
with no ability to convert speech to text and then text to speech in another
language. This project explores the idea of translating speech directly into a
different language, bypassing the intermediate text form, and acknowledges
the significant challenge this poses due to the high dimensional nature of speech
data. To tackle this, we propose new types of cross-domain alignments and a
comprehensive system that can learn to perform this complex task. Despite having
no training data for a particular language pair, our system is able to
demonstrate its capabilities on a previously untried Spanish to French speech
translation task, with a notable gap remaining between human and machine
performance. Notably, our system achieves this zero-shot translation capability
without the need for additional parameters in relation to multilingual speechto-speech translation models. Our findings validate the potential of this zero-shot speech translation approach, with potential future improvements to be
gained from a more extensive system evaluation and a more intricate model
architecture. Our code is available at https://github.com/parag-sitajit/zero-shot-speech-translation. Our model performance is presented at tab.1 of our paper and the audio samples for our evaluation are available at https://speechkitten.github.io/zero-shot-speech-translation/, with more detailed information available in our paper "Zero-shot Speech Translation" (arXiv 2206.15031). Birtel's proof that a complex, smooth, 4-dimensional manifold hosts an infinite number of smoothly embedded, trefoil-shaped tori has significant implications for our current understanding of the quantum topological invariants known as TQFTs. His discovery demonstrates that these invariants cannot be represented by altering a single component in a way that changes the genus of the shape. Our research extends this finding by showing that removing or adding multiple non-intersecting, genus-zero tori does not affect a smooth, 4-dimensional manifold's ability to support a representation of the Heisenberg algebra, a fundamental component of many TQFTs. This means that a wide range of TQFTs can still be defined on such altered manifolds. Additionally, our proof confirms that birational alterations maintain the properties of a point on a smooth, 4-dimensional manifold known as a Soergel's variable. Furthermore, our research allows us to define representations of the Heisenberg algebra for a broader category of smooth, 4-dimensional manifolds, thereby expanding the reach of many TQFTs. The specific TQFTs that can be applied to these altered manifolds include versions of the Chern-Simons, Jones, and Kauffman invariants. Our proof's methods also provide a path to proving the correctness of these definitions in an automated fashion. Our research also identifies a relationship between the representations of the Heisenberg algebra and the properties of a different mathematical structure known as a Soergel's variable, which may have value in future studies. Our proof's main argument relies on a complicated set of calculations involving many intersecting, genus-one tori, which can be seen as a complex, higher-dimensional version of the trefoil-shaped tori originally considered by Birtel. Our proof's findings provide the basis for exploring whether similar relationships between quantum and classical topological invariants exist in higher-dimensional manifolds. Using deep learning on images can be an effective way to detect diseases, specifically cardiovascular diseases, by analyzing chest X-rays. However, accessing high-quality medical images labeled with cardiovascular disease diagnoses can be challenging due to data privacy restrictions and the need for primary expert diagnoses. Instead of relying on secondary diagnoses from radiology reports, which can be time-consuming and inconsistent, we propose a different approach. By training a deep learning model on edited chest X-ray images along with their associated radiology reports, we can utilize the existing dataset while also protecting patient confidentiality. The model learns to detect diseases directly from the images and uses the edits to ensure the models are illness-aware, reducing the risk of overfitting on report-based features rather than visual signs of diseases. By testing our deep learning framework on the CheXpert dataset, we found that a pre-trained DenseASPP model achieved high accuracy in detecting five specific cardiovascular disease diagnoses when trained with edited images. Moreover, the results showed that the highest performing models were those trained with edited images that aligned with the radiology reports, demonstrating the effectiveness of our illness-aware image modification approach. The modified dataset and associated code are available for use and adaptation by other researchers. The changes made to the images are reversible and do not add any new identifying information, further ensuring patient confidentiality is maintained. The existing dataset can be used as is, without the need for further data collection or primary expert diagnoses. The code and the modified dataset can be found at the following link https://github.com/seyedmohammadghasemi/illness-aware-image-modification, where the pre-trained models can be found in the models folder. The CheXpert dataset used in this study can be downloaded from https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.04043, where the original paper was published in the conference, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31: Automatic Machine Learning Track, 2023. The original paper titled, Multi-Task Learning of Cardiomegaly Detection from Chest X-rays, was published in the journal, IEEE Access, Volume 9, 2021. The original paper titled, Automatic detection of pulmonary nodules in lung images via deep learning, was published in the journal, Journal of Medical Signals and Systems, Volume 9, Issue 2, 2021. visualizing high-dimensional data,  facilitating both data understanding and
identification of key features,  yet their limitations in capturing non-linear
relationships lead to a need for more comprehensive visualization tools.  At their
core, many advanced visualization methods in machine learning, such as t-SNE and
UMAP, are essentially non-linear versions of PCA,  however these techniques do not
directly enable feature analysis.  To address these shortcomings,  ViDaExpert
integrates a range of visualization techniques,  including t-SNE, UMAP, Autoencoders
and ViDa,  allowing for both holistic data understanding and detailed feature
examination.  Developed with a user-friendly interface in mind,  ViDaExpert also
offers customizable visualization tools and a feature inspector for in-depth
analysis of target data points,  making it a user-friendly and versatile data
visualization tool.  Additionally,  ViDaExpert includes a data point picker and
a results dashboard for easy exploration of the visualized data.  To utilize

format types,  or load their data via a pandas DataFrame.  As an open-source

This research provides a thorough analysis of the rapid determination of signed distance functions for individuals using Newtonian potentials on flat regions. Our method is fully explicit, easy to implement, and effective in both theoretical and practical terms. We have incorporated our technique into an efficient, wide-ranging simulation framework called the Newton Buggy Simulator (NBS). By applying our distance calculation method, we've also developed a straightforward collision detection algorithm that serves NBS well. Our research also covers a concise proof of a related Lax-Milgram type theorem. This work was initially presented at the 2019 SC19 conference. Since then, we've made some minor corrections to the NBS system and rewritten the proof, which we've included here. Although we've focused on a specific application, our rapid distance calculation method can be adapted to other contexts. Our approach has since been the basis for further research described in a separate paper also presented at the 2019 SC19 conference. That study explored various force fields while confirming that some of them result in chaotic behavior in the NBS system. Our subsequent research, which has been ongoing, has led to an even more efficient version of the NBS simulator. That version utilized a less precise distance calculation method and was shown at the 2020 SIAM Conference on Computational Science and Engineering. Our current research continues to investigate the properties of the NBS simulator using a variant of the Newton Buggy Simulator called the Newton Newton Buggy Simulator (NNBS). Our NNBS system features a more precise distance calculation method that we've successfully adapted for use with multiple individuals. This new version of the NNBS simulator uses a variant of the fast Newton transform that we've coined the sparse Newton transform (SNT). Our experience with the SNT has been positive, resulting in a significant reduction in costs associated with the evaluation of Newton potentials in the NNBS system. Our research with the NNBS simulator has also led to the identification of some known results through the application of new techniques such as Blaschke's theorem and mass transfer.
